title: Fever and earache in a three-year-old

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, come on in. And this must be Poppy?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Yes, this is Poppy. I'm her mum, Gemma.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello Poppy. That's a lovely rabbit. What's been happening?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She's had a temperature and she keeps pulling at her ear. She was up most of last night crying.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long has she had the temperature?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Since Tuesday night, so two days. No, hang on, it was Monday. It was the night of her swimming lesson, so Monday evening. Three days.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, since Monday evening. Have you measured it?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: It was 38.9 last night on the ear thermometer.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Which ear has she been pulling at?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: The right one, mostly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My ear hurts.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Poor you, Poppy. Is she eating and drinking?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Not eating much, but she's drinking okay. Juice and milk.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Wet nappies, or is she out of nappies now?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She's in pants in the day. She's still weeing normally, a few times today already.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any vomiting or diarrhoea?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She was sick once on Tuesday, but not since. No diarrhoea.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any cough or runny nose?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: A runny nose for about a week, before all this started.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any rash at all?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No, I've checked. Her brother had chickenpox two weeks ago, so I've been watching her like a hawk, but nothing.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Good thinking. Has she had chickenpox herself?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No, never. We're expecting it any day.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Has she been more sleepy than usual, or hard to wake?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No, she's grumpy but she's herself. She was playing with her brother this morning.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any problems breathing?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any medical problems, and is she up to date with her jabs?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She's healthy, and yes, all her vaccinations are done.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Does she take any medicines regularly, and any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No regular medicines, and no allergies.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What have you been giving her for the temperature?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Calpol, but only when she seems really bad.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay. Let me examine her. Poppy, can I look at your rabbit's ears first? Good. She weighs 14 kilograms on the scales. Her temperature is 38.4, heart rate 130, breathing rate 26. Her hands and feet are warm and the capillary refill is under two seconds. She's alert and chatting to me.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Rabbit's ears are fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: They are! Now your ears. The left eardrum looks normal. The right eardrum is red and bulging. Can you say ahh? Her throat is a little red. Let me listen to your chest. That's clear. No rash on her skin.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Is it an ear infection?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Yes, it looks like a middle ear infection on the right side. Most of these get better on their own within three days or so, even without antibiotics, and antibiotics don't make much difference to the pain.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Oh. I thought she'd need antibiotics.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What I'd suggest is giving her paracetamol and ibuprofen regularly for the pain, rather than only when she seems bad. For Poppy that's paracetamol 180 milligrams, which is 7.5 millilitres of the 120 milligrams in 5 millilitres infant suspension, up to four times a day. And ibuprofen 100 milligrams, that's 5 millilitres of the 100 milligrams in 5 millilitres suspension, three times a day with food.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay. Can I give both?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Yes, you can give both. I'll also do a back-up prescription for amoxicillin, 250 milligrams three times a day for 5 days. Only collect it if she's not improving after three days, or sooner if she's getting worse.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Now, it's important to know when to get help urgently. If she gets a rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass on it, if she becomes very drowsy or hard to wake, if she's struggling to breathe, or if she stops drinking and isn't weeing, call 999 or go straight to A&E.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And if the fever lasts more than five days in total, if you notice any discharge from her ear, or she's not improving after three days, contact us or 111.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Thank you. And with the chickenpox, should I do anything?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: She may well get it in the next week or so, since she's been exposed. If she does, and she seems very unwell with it, let us know. There's information in the leaflet I'll give you.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Thank you, doctor.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Bye bye.

reference_note.history: Fever since Monday evening (3 days), maximum 38.9 °C at home. Pulling at the right ear, unsettled overnight. Eating less but drinking well; passing urine normally. Vomited once on Tuesday, none since. No diarrhoea. Coryza for about a week preceding. No rash. Her brother had chickenpox two weeks ago; she has not had chickenpox. Alert and playing this morning. No breathing difficulty. Previously well; immunisations up to date. Paracetamol given intermittently.
reference_note.medications_allergies: No regular medications. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: Weight 14 kg. Temperature 38.4 °C, HR 130, RR 26. Warm peripheries, CRT under 2 seconds. Alert and interactive. Left tympanic membrane normal. Right tympanic membrane red and bulging. Throat mildly erythematous. Chest clear. No rash.
reference_note.impression: Right acute otitis media. No features of serious bacterial illness. Recent chickenpox contact.
reference_note.plan: Regular analgesia: paracetamol 180 mg (7.5 mL of 120 mg/5 mL) up to four times daily and ibuprofen 100 mg (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times daily with food. Back-up prescription: amoxicillin 250 mg three times daily for 5 days, to collect only if not improving after 3 days or if worsening. Leaflet on chickenpox given.
reference_note.safety_netting: Call 999 or attend A&E if a non-blanching rash, very drowsy or difficult to rouse, breathing difficulty, or not drinking and not passing urine. Contact GP or 111 if fever lasts more than 5 days in total, ear discharge, or not improving after 3 days. Report if develops chickenpox and seems very unwell.
